issues.legal_issue: A landlord-owner seeking possession of non-residential accommodation under the special bona fide-requirement procedure need not plead ownership or independently prove it to succeed.
material_facts: The landlord applied for possession of a shop, saying it was needed to start a business for her sons.
The tenant disputed the landlord’s ownership and bona fide requirement.
The Rent Controller found for the landlord on ownership and bona fide requirement, but the High Court set aside the eviction order because it considered independent proof of ownership necessary.

The special procedure provided for a tenant to obtain leave to contest and treated the landlord’s statements as admitted if leave was not obtained; it also presumed bona fide requirement unless the contrary was proved.
issues.conclusion: The ownership language in Section 23A(b) enables an owner-landlord to apply for possession; it does not require the landlord to plead ownership or adduce independent evidence proving it. A tenant may contest ownership only if not barred from doing so by tenant’s estoppel.
issues.legal_principle: Reading Section 23A(b) in the context of the expedited procedure in Sections 23B, 23C and 23D, the court held that requiring a separate pleading and proof of ownership would frustrate the legislative scheme. Section 116 of the Evidence Act may prevent a tenant from denying the landlord’s title. The court referred to Stringer’s Estate, Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath and Krishna v. Barabani Coal Concern Ltd. It also observed that a landlord seeking possession on the same ground under Section 12(1)(f) was not required to plead and prove ownership in that manner.

predicates.special_nonresidential_eviction_proceedi: A landlord seeks possession of non-residential accommodation through a special procedure based on bona fide need for a business.
predicates.landlord_is_owner: The applicant landlord owns the accommodation for which possession is sought.

issues.definition: When an owner seeks possession of non-residential accommodation through the special business-need procedure, separate pleading or independent proof of ownership is not required.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who accepts a subsequent landlord as landlord cannot later deny that landlord’s title when the subsequent landlord seeks possession, if the tenant is not otherwise entitled to deny that title.
material_facts: The tenant initially occupied the shop as tenant of its former owner.
The former owner told the tenant that ownership had passed to the landlord and that the landlord was thereafter the tenant’s landlord.
The tenant addressed a notice to the landlord and stated in a civil plaint that the landlord had become the owner; the tenant also sent rent to the landlord.
When the landlord later sought possession, the tenant denied her ownership.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was estopped from denying the landlord’s title because he had acknowledged her as landlord by his conduct and statements.
issues.legal_principle: Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, bars a tenant, during the tenancy, from denying that the landlord had title at the beginning of the tenancy. The court held that the estoppel also applies where a person already in possession as a tenant acknowledges a subsequent landlord who derives title from the former landlord. It relied on Stringer’s Estate, Sri Ram Pasricha v. Jagannath and Krishna v. Barabani Coal Concern Ltd.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_by_subsequent_landlo: A landlord who became entitled to the property after the tenancy began seeks possession from the tenant.
predicates.tenant_accepted_subsequent_landlord: The tenant acknowledged the subsequent landlord as landlord through statements or conduct.
predicates.title_derived_from_former_landlord: The subsequent landlord derived title from the person who was the landlord when the tenancy began.

issues.definition: When a tenant accepts a subsequent landlord whose title derives from the former landlord, the tenant cannot deny that subsequent landlord’s title in a possession proceeding.
